subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Neutron Stars: Supernova Leftovers
description: A quick, practical guide to Neutron Stars: Supernova Leftovers.

hook.text: When a massive star's core collapses in a supernova, what's left is a neutron star—a city-sized ball of nuclear matter.

buildup.text: A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere just 20 km across. A teaspoon weighs a billion tons.

discovery.text: Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered the first pulsar in 1967—a spinning neutron star emitting regular radio pulses.

twist.text: Some neutron stars spin hundreds of times per second. Millisecond pulsars are the most precise natural clocks in the universe.

climax.text: Magnetars are neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields—a trillion times stronger than Earth's. They can crack their own crust.

punchline.text: A billion tons per teaspoon. Spinning hundreds of times a second.

quiz.question: What is a magnetar?
options: A neutron star with an extremely powerful magnetic field, trillions of times stronger than Earth's
A type of black hole that emits strong magnetic radiation
A star that uses magnetic energy instead of nuclear fusion for power

details.summary: Neutron stars are the ultra-dense cores left after massive stars explode as supernovae. A teaspoon of neutron star material weighs about a billion tons. Roughly 20 km across but containing 1-2 solar masses, they spin up to hundreds of times per second and many emit beams of radiation as pulsars.
details.whyItMatters: Neutron stars are nature's densest observable objects. They serve as cosmic laboratories for testing nuclear physics, general relativity, and the behavior of matter under conditions impossible to recreate on Earth.
takeaways: Ultra-dense remnants just 20 km across with 1-2 solar masses
A teaspoon weighs about a billion tons
Many spin rapidly and emit radiation as pulsars

faq.question: What happens if matter falls onto a neutron star?
faq.answer: Infalling matter is compressed and heated to millions of degrees, often producing X-ray bursts as hydrogen and helium undergo thermonuclear explosions on the surface. These bursts last seconds and repeat periodically. The magnetic field channels matter toward the poles.

faq.question: What is neutron star matter actually like?
faq.answer: The outer crust is crystallized iron nuclei. Deeper, nuclei become increasingly neutron-rich. Below about 1 km depth, nuclei dissolve into a sea of neutrons with a few protons and electrons. The core may contain exotic matter: quark soup, hyperons, or superfluids.
